source.title: Superposition disentanglement of neural representations reveals hidden alignment
source.authors: André Longon; D. Klindt; Meenakshi Khosla

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests superposition and its consequences using toy autoencoders, SAE disentanglement, and alignment measures; it does not reproduce the original study's full method or test its sparsity/geometry predictions directly.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own measurements of toy-model feature coverage and arrangements, alignment before and after SAE encoding, and DNN-to-brain alignment. The paper also gives theoretical arguments and cites results from other work; those are not recorded as empirical rows. Most plotted numeric values are not stated in the text, so the relevant row values are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The paper mainly uses toy-model superposition as a tool to study alignment metrics. Its own toy autoencoders still report how many of 64 sparse features are represented by 8, 16 or 32 neurons, which bears on V1 (more features than dimensions) and, weakly, on V2 (coverage limited by capacity). The SAE alignment, DNN and brain results measure alignment rather than superposition itself.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that different superposition arrangements deflate predictive-mapping alignment and that SAE disentanglement typically raises it in toy models, deep DNN layers and DNN→brain regression. They argue disentanglement is necessary to reveal true alignment. They caveat that DNN arrangements are unverifiable and that SAEs may construct new representations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses toy autoencoders following the methodology of Toy Models of Superposition, but with a task-importance-weighted reconstruction loss, a 10% feature activation probability, and a focus on cross-model alignment and SAE disentanglement rather than reproducing the original analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model depth and architecture: ResNet50 decreases at the intermediate layer but increases at the deep layer; ViT-B/16 improves at both tested layers, with a larger deep-layer gain. Toy-model SAE soft-matching decreases at N=8 but increases at N=16 and N=32. Regression results depend on whether SAE latents are used on one side or both.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy models, the same shared features take different superposition arrangements across seeds: almost all neurons have a maximum semi-matching correlation below 0.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition arrangements of shared features are not unique and vary with random initialization.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing neurons with SAE latents changes cross-model alignment. Soft-matching falls at N=8 and in the ResNet50 intermediate layer, and rises elsewhere. SAE→Neuron regression is generally higher than the neuron baseline, while SAE→SAE regression is mostly lower.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE disentanglement can raise measured representational alignment, depending on capacity, layer and metric.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE latents of vision DNNs predict human ventral-stream fMRI better than neurons do: ResNet50 +13.9%, ViT +3.5%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Disentangling DNN representations with SAEs improves DNN-to-brain linear predictivity.

record.problems: Real DNN superposition arrangements and ground-truth features cannot be verified directly. The authors acknowledge SAE reconstruction, consistency, absorption, and identifiability limitations, and do not exhaustively compare SAE architectures. Real-model and DNN-to-brain results are limited in scope; many plotted numerical values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows omitted. Figure-only control values are retained where the text identifies the control, but their outcomes cannot be determined from the prose.

untested.parts: Near-orthogonality of feature directions, the sparsity-dependent phase transition (only one sparsity, 10%, is used), and regular geometric arrangements.
Whether important features get dedicated dimensions while others share them; polysemanticity as the direct outcome of capacity competition.
Not tested. The real models are vision DNNs, not LLMs, and their features cannot be verified.
Not tested. The authors cite SAE consistency, absorption and identifiability limits.

missing.what: Validation that SAE latents match ground-truth toy features better than neurons do, with the gap growing with N.
missing.versions: none (closest to V1/V5, but toy-model SAE recovery is not covered by any version)

missing.what: Semi-matching alignment results for the toy models and DNNs, said to be highly consistent with soft-matching.

record.verdict_notes: Superposition is mainly a tool here. Only the toy-model feature-coverage rows bear on the versions, and only at one sparsity level. The reader's links from the SAE alignment rows to V1 were removed because they measure alignment, not superposition geometry.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether directions are nearly orthogonal, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometric arrangements. Toy-model results show differing arrangements and alignment changes, not the full geometry claim.

Measures feature coverage as neuron count changes, but does not report whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while less important features share them, or directly test polysemanticity as the cause.
Does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The real networks studied are visual DNNs, not LLMs; the study also cannot verify feature spreading or SAE feature recovery directly in those real networks.
Does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units. It notes known SAE limitations and that its own results cannot verify disentanglement in DNNs.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.
